Prader-Willi syndrome as an approved indication is specific to Genotropin's own FDA label, not a somatropin-class-wide indication; independent general drug references (e.g., Mayo Clinic's pooled somatropin monograph, checked 2026-08-29) frame PWS only as a contraindication subgroup (children who are severely obese or have severe respiratory impairment), not as a labeled indication, because such references pool multiple brands. Do not present PWS as uniformly an approved use across all somatropin products.

claims.statement: Genotropin labeling describes an adult GHD weight-based dosing protocol: initial dose not more than 0.04 mg/kg/week, titrated upward as tolerated to a maximum of 0.08 mg/kg/week at 4-8 week intervals; the label also specifies that Genotropin must be given subcutaneously and must not be injected intravenously. This is trial/label protocol context only and is not a use recommendation.

claims.statement: Following the SAGhE French cohort study that raised a possible mortality signal in patients treated with recombinant human growth hormone during childhood, FDA reviewed the study alongside other data sources and concluded the evidence for an increased risk of death was inconclusive due to design weaknesses in SAGhE, and that available medical literature and adverse event reports did not otherwise support a mortality link; FDA advised continuing to prescribe and use recombinant human growth hormone according to labeled recommendations while its review continued. A subsequent 2020 SAGhE cohort follow-up study (The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology; 24,232 patients, over 400,000 patient-years of follow-up) found that all-cause mortality was not significantly increased in low-risk patients with isolated growth hormone deficiency or idiopathic short stature (SMR 1.1, 95% CI 0.9-1.3), while cause-specific mortality from diseases of the circulatory and haematological systems was increased across all risk groups, indicating the elevated mortality seen in moderate/high-risk groups tracks underlying diagnosis rather than growth hormone treatment itself, but warranting continued monitoring of circulatory/haematological causes.

context.population: patients treated with recombinant human growth hormone, particularly during childhood
context.formulation: recombinant human growth hormone products generally

extractedEvidence.quote: The evidence regarding recombinant human growth hormone and increased risk of death is inconclusive.

claims.statement: A systematic review of 27 randomized controlled trials (n=440) of growth hormone in healthy, physically fit young adults found GH increased lean body mass but had minimal effect on key measures of athletic performance (no significant improvement in strength across multiple muscle groups or in VO2max), and was associated with higher rates of adverse events - soft tissue swelling in 44% vs 1% of controls and fatigue in 35% vs 0% - plus elevated exercise lactate suggestive of impaired rather than enhanced exercise capacity.

conflicts.summary: The SAGhE French cohort study raised a possible increased mortality signal associated with recombinant human growth hormone in patients treated during childhood, but FDA's own safety review concluded the evidence was inconclusive due to study design weaknesses and directed continued use per labeling. This packet did not locate a definitive later FDA communication closing out the signal. Updated 2026-08-29: a 2020 SAGhE cohort follow-up (Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, PMID 32707116; 24,232 patients, 400,000+ patient-years) was independently fetched and added -- it found no significantly increased all-cause mortality in low-risk GHD/idiopathic-short-stature patients (SMR 1.1), with elevated mortality in higher-risk groups tracking underlying diagnosis rather than treatment, but it also identified a residual increase in cause-specific circulatory/haematological mortality across all risk groups. This narrows but does not fully close the tension between the epidemiological signal and FDA's inconclusive determination, since no later FDA communication addressing this newer data was located; still needs human review against the most current FDA safety communications at review time.

reviewReasons: Expansion-batch evidence packet requires human review before publication.

Resolved 2026-08-29: SAGhE mortality safety-signal was anchored only to the 2011-2012 FDA communication; added the 2020 SAGhE cohort follow-up (Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, PMID 32707116), independently fetched and verbatim-quoted this session, to the claim and conflict record. No later definitive FDA communication closing out the original signal was located, so this remains flagged for human review as a safety-critical, fieldAuthorityRequired claim.
